items.e: THE MOUNTAIN OF GOD, UNTO HOREB. This is the manner in which Moses recorded it. The place is called Horeb because of its great heat and lack of rainfall. As Moses noted, it is located three days’ journey from Egypt. There is no moisture there and the dryness is overpowering because the Nile is far away.

APPEARED. Some interpret be-labbat esh to mean: in a flame of fire. However, it appears to me that its meaning is, in the heart of the fire, for we indeed find, How weak is thy heart (libbatekh) (Ezek. 16:30). However, Rabbi Adonim says that if this were so, then be-labbat would have been vocalized with a chirik beneath the lamed like the word ginnat (garden of) in I went down into the garden of nuts (Canticles 6:11). Now, Rabbi Adonim seems to have forgotten the word gannah (garden) in And as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth (Is. 61:11).

THE BUSH. Saadiah Gaon says that seneh (bush) is a type of thorn bush. He further explains that the word seneh in And the good will of Him that dwelt (shokhni) in the bush (seneh) (Deut. 33:16) means heaven; that is, it refers to God the glorious. Rabbi Joshua, on the other hand, says that the verse refers to the glory that dwelt in the bush. However, Rabbi Joshua spoke incorrectly, for how can God be called “Him that dwelleth in the bush” when he dwelt there for but a moment. Furthermore, why is the word shokhni (dwelt) in the po’el form? The word oseh (makes) in Who makes (oseh) heaven and earth (Ps. 121:2) is different, as God is constantly making and causing heaven and earth to exist in the same manner as speech issues from the mouth of man. Additionally, after mentioning all the precious things (Deut. 33:13-16), Scripture concludes with the good will of God . Moreover, what reason is there to mention this angel? Furthermore, Scripture should have read, ba-seneh (in the bush) and thereby would have referred to the well-known bush.In my opinion seneh (bush) refers to only one thing, namely, a type of dry thorn bush. This is the case in Arabic. Mount Sinai is so named because this type of bush grew there. Similarly, its interpretation is: and the good will that he who lives in the place of the bush ( seneh ) seeks; that is, a person living in such a place entreats and prays that God do his will and wet the land that he lives in. He prays that God change it from a dry place, a place where the seneh grows, to an amply watered place so that it becomes like a wet and well-watered garden. Scripture states that an angel of the Lord appeared out of the midst of the bush . The word seneh has the definite article the ( heh ) prefixed to it because these are Moses’ very own words in writing the Torah.The word bo’er (burned) is a transitive verb. The phrase a burning fire is similar to a devouring fire (Deut. 4:24). As the fire that burneth (tivar) the forest (Ps. 83:15) is proof of this. Now the fire that burned in the bush devoured all that was around it. Our verse is similar to They have set Thy sanctuary on fire (Ps. 74:7). While the mountain did burn with fire (Deut. 5:20) is also similar.

[WAS NOT CONSUMED.] The word ukkal (consumed) is an adjective. It is similar to the pa’ul . The words lukkach (taken), which is vocalized with a kamatz in if thou see me when I am taken (II Kings 2:10), yullad (shall be born) in unto the child that shall be born (Jud. 13:8), yukashim (snared) in even so are the sons of man snared (Eccles. 9:12) are similar. Now since these verbs are transitive, the word mu’edet (unsteady) in and an unsteady leg (Prov. 25:19) cannot be classified among these words as these words are transitive. Mu’edet is similar to mo’edet , a po’elet , with the exception that a shuruk has been substituted for a cholam .

AND MOSES SAID: I WILL TURN ASIDE ( ASURAH ) NOW. When a verb from the root samekh, vav, resh is followed by a mem it means: to distance from, as in suru mi-menni (turn aside from me) (Ps. 6:9) in which the speaker says, distance yourself from me. However, if the word el (to) which is vocalized with a segol follows it, then it has the opposite meaning, as in suru elai (turn in) (Jud. 4:18), the meaning of which is, turn from your place and come to me. Moses wanted to turn aside from where he was and to then draw near to the bush.

AND SEE THIS GREAT SIGHT. This is the first sign recorded in the Torah that the Lord did via his prophet Moses. Scripture thus says, and this shall be the token (sign) unto thee that I have sent thee (v. 12). Yefet says that the interpretation of the sign is as follows: the enemy is compared to fire and Israel to a bush. Hence the bush was not burnt.

AND WHEN THE LORD SAW. These words were also written later by Moses. The angel was called by God’s revered name in the sense of, for My name is in him (Ex. 23:21). I will explain this when I comment on the latter verse. We find the same with the angel that appeared to Gideon. There it is written, And the Lord said unto him (Jud. 6:23). Or its meaning is that the Lord saw that Moses turned aside to see the great sight and He commanded an angel to call Moses. Hence the use of the term elohim (God) in our verse. The name Elohim is not a proper name but is, as I will explain, an adjective. It pertains to all holy beings that are incorporeal and are not forces in a body, as it is written, except the angels , whose dwelling is not with flesh (Dan. 2:11), that is, with a body. Thus elohim refers to the above-noted angel.

AND HE SAID: DRAW NOT NIGH HITHER. Its meaning is, stand in your place and draw not nigh to the bush where the fire is. Is there yet a man come hither? (I Sam. 10:22) is similar. A nun is missing in the word shal (put off), as it is in the word ga (touch), for the word shal comes from the same root as ve-nashal (and shall cast out) in and shall cast out many nations (Deut. 7:1).

MOREOVER HE SAID: I AM THE LORD OF THY FATHER. After stating, I am the God of thy father , He explains that the reference is to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He starts with Abraham because Abraham was the first to call upon the name of the Lord and he built an altar to the Lord, for his father and his brother worshipped idols. These three are mentioned while those closest to Moses, namely, Levi, Kehat, and Amram, are not noted because the former were prophets. Furthermore, they were fathers of all of Israel. Levi was not, whereas Moses stood for all of Israel. When God told Moses, I am the God of thy father , He was, as it were, speaking to all of Israel because Moses represented Israel.

AND MOSES HID HIS FACE. This is similar to for I have seen God face, to face, and my life is preserved (Gen. 32:31). The sensory perception of the eye is like the gate of heaven, for it can see in one moment images that are both far and near. However, this is not the case with the senses of the ears, nose, palate, and hand. Moses hid his face because he was greatly afraid.
AND THE LORD SAID. The messenger speaks the same language as the one who sent him.
[I HAVE SURELY SEEN.] Its meaning is: I have seen that which people do not see, namely, the violence that is done to them secretly.
AND HAVE HEARD THEIR CRY. I have heard their cry which is heard by all and I know the pain which they bear in their hearts.

AND I AM COME DOWN. Scripture says this because the heavens are more glorious than the earth. God’s glory fills everything. It is only because the decrees come down from heaven that Scripture employs the term And I am come down . Furthermore, the angel was a higher form and Moses was not able to go up to heaven. Hence Scripture reads, and I am come down to save my people.

AND TO BRING THEM UP. This is in contrast to and I am come down . As I dwell in a high place so will I cause them to dwell in the most elevated place that is upon the earth. The aforementioned are the words of the angel. It is likewise written, He made him ride on the high places of the earth (Deut. 32:13). Behold, the Israelites went out of a land where they were afflicted to a good land. Scripture does not mention the Girgashites because they were the smallest of the seven. Now, it is fitting to raise the following question: Since six nations were descended from Canaan, why does Scripture mention the Canaanites? The answer is: The term Canaanites is an ethnic name and includes all the nations living in Canaan. Hence the entire land was called the land of Canaan. The Perizzite is to be identified with Sidon. The rest of the sons of Canaan mentioned in Scripture were few in number and are included in the term Canaanite.
AND NOW, BEHOLD. Its meaning is: And now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel who have repented is come unto Me.

[MOREOVER I HAVE SEEN THE OPPRESSION.] Its meaning is: Moreover I have seen the oppression with which they in their pride oppress them. Jethro similarly said, for that they dealt proudly against them (Ex. 18:11).
COME NOW THEREFORE. As My messenger to Pharaoh.

AND MOSES SAID…WHO AM I. There is no difference between the words ani (I) and anokhi (I). The latter are similar to immi (with me) and immadi (with me). We have found that it is the way of the Hebrew tongue to derive the word ani (I) and the words attah (you in the singular) and attem (you in the plural), whose nuns have been swallowed, from the root of an (whither) in Whither went ye (I Sam. 10:14), as the place indicates the speaker. It is possible that the word anokhi is derived from the root of anakh (plumbline) (Amos 7:7) in a manner similar to the derivation of the word nechushtekh (thy bottom) (Ezek. 16:36).Because the Lord told Moses, come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh (v. 10), Moses responded, I am a shepherd and Pharaoh is a great king.Because God told Moses, that thou mayest bring forth My people the children of Israel out of Egypt (v. 10), Moses answered the Lord, Who am I that I am able to bring forth a great nation such as the children of Israel out of Egypt .

AND HE SAID: CERTAINLY I WILL BE WITH THEE. Now go to Pharaoh and bring out the children of Israel and behold, I have given you a token that I have sent you. The reason they are being brought out of Egypt is that they should serve Me on this mountain where I have shown you this great wonder. It is thus written, ( I am the Lord ) …that brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God (Lev. 22:23). Moses similarly said to Pharaoh, We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to the Lord our God (Ex. 8:23) because the latter is the walking distance between eastern Egypt and Mount Sinai. However, when Israel left Egypt they did not go there via the land of the Philistines. Furthermore, Israel, as I will explain, dwelt in one place for many days. It is precisely this that Moses spoke of when he wrote, and (Moses) builded an altar under the mount…and…offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings (Ex. 24:4, 5). He then made a covenant with Israel that they be a people unto the Lord and that the Lord be their God.

AND MOSES SAID. Moses now asked which of God’s names he should relate to Israel, for with the name of El Shaddai (God Almighty) he could not perform signs. The latter are only performed with God’s great and glorious name. Rabbi Joshua says that the Israelites had a tradition from their forefathers that Israel’s savior would reveal a new name of God to them, a name that they had never heard. Now when Rabbi Joshua heard that Scripture states, I am the Lord that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees (Gen. 15:7), he explained it by saying that these are the words of Moses. However, Rabbi Joshua is mistaken. In the Torah portion Bereshit at the beginning of the Pentateuch we find that Scripture does not employ the Tetragrammaton but uses the name Elohim (God) until the verse which concludes with the words in creating had made (Gen. 2:3). After the latter verse Scripture refers to God by the name Adonai Elohim (Lord God). After the birth of Cain, Scripture employs the term Adonai (Lord) for the Deity only by itself. We never find Moses using the name Elohim for God. Moses always refers to Him by His great and glorious name. He uses the term Elohim only in one place. He does this because Pharaoh said, Entreat the Lord, and let there be enough of God’s (Elohim) thunderings (Ex. 9:28). Upon hearing this, Moses responded, I know that ye will not fear the Lord (Adonai Elohim) (Ex. 9:30). However, there is no other similar case in Scripture.

AND GOD SAID…I AM. Its meaning is, That I Am. Compare, And the house of David shall be as God, As the angel of the Lord before them (Zech. 12:8). Angel of the Lord , which follows God , explains the term God .

AND GOD SAID MOREOVER…THE LORD. Another name meaning the same as the first one. However, one name ( EHYH ) is in the first person and this name ( YHVH ) is in the third person. It comes from the same root as yah (Lord). These three names are proper names. I will now go on to explain the meaning of the proper name of God, the meaning of its letters, part of the secret of God’s glorious name, and why it is not read as written.

The words of Abraham the author: Behold, I now begin to elaborate because I need a firm foundation. Note that a proper name serves as a token and as a sign of the one being referred to by those who enunciate it and those who hear it. A proper name is distinguished from an adjective in four ways. The first is that an adjective is derived from an imperative, such as chakham (be wise) in My son, be wise (Prov. 27:11), or a perfect, as in My son, if your heart gets wisdom (chakham) (Prov. 23:15), or an imperfect, as in That thou mayest be wise (techkam) in thy latter end (Prov. 19:20). However, this is not the case with a proper noun such as Abraham, as no perfect or imperfect form can be derived from it. Now even though there are proper nouns that are derived from verbs, such as the name yitzchak (Isaac), we do not say yitzchakti (I was Isaaced) or itzchak (I will be Isaaced). A proper name is not used as an adjective. The second difference is that an adjective comes in the plural. For example, chakham (wise) becomes chakhamim (wise). However, we do not have a plural form for the proper name avraham (Abraham). Thus we do not say avrahamim (Abrahams). Neither is there a plural for the proper name yisra’el (Israel). Thus if there are two people named Israel in a place we do not say yisra’elim (Israels). We would only use the term yisra’elim if we wanted to relate each of them to the people of Israel, as the term Israel is the name of a group. The third difference is that a definite article is not prefixed to a proper noun as it is to an adjective. From the word chakham (wise) we get he-chakham (the wise man) (Eccles. 2:14). However, it is incorrect to say ha-avraham (the Abraham) or ha-yitzchak (the Isaac). The word ha-kohelet (Eccles. 12:8) cannot be used as an argument against the aforementioned because the term kohelet is not a proper name but an adjective describing the wisdom which was accumulated. Similarly, the word va-ha-adam (Gen. 2:8) is an adjective. It has a secret meaning to it, as it is the name of a genus. The name ha-menasheh (Deut. 3:13) has a definite article before it because it refers to genealogy. The fourth difference is that a proper noun has no construct form whereas an adjective does. For example, we find, chakham lev (wise of heart) (Job 9:4). However, it would be incorrect to say yitzchak ha-dor (Isaac of the generation), because a proper name stands by itself. The same is the case with the name Eheyeh (I am) and also with the glorious name of God, the Tetragrammaton, because both of these names are proper names. Now, we do find, Adonai tzeva’ot (the Lord of hosts) (Is. 1:9), and as a result many were forced to conclude that tzeva’ot is a proper name or that the Lord is outstanding among His host. However, this is incorrect, because Scripture reads, Elohe ha-tzeva’ot (the God of Hosts) (Amos 3:13). Tzeva’ot is never encountered by itself. It is always connected either to the word Elohim (God) or to God’s glorious name, Adonai ( Elohim ). Do not be bothered by the phrase Adonai Elohim tzeva’ot (O Lord God of hosts) (Ps. 59:6), as its meaning is similar to ve-ha-nevu’ah oded ha-navi (even the prophecy of Oded the prophet) (II Chron. 15:8).

Now the Lord’s personal name is sometimes used in an adjectival sense because God alone exists forever and the existence of all things is contingent upon Him. God’s proper name is used here in the same way that the name moshe (Moses) is used in Then He remembered the days of old, when He drew (moshe) His people (Is. 63:11). The meaning of Adonai when used as an adjective is: the maintainer of existence. Hence in the phrase Adonai Elohim the holy angels are connected to God. Similarly, in the phrase Adonai tzeva’ot (Lord of hosts) tzeva’ot refers to the hosts of heaven. Pay no attention to Saadiah Gaon who says that God is called Adonai tzeva’ot because of Israel. Saadiah offers proof from and I will…bring forth My hosts (tzivotai), My people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt (Ex. 7:4). However, look at I saw the Lord sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him (I Kings 22:19). Now the name Elohim is an adjective, because it comes in both the plural and the singular. Compare, Is not God (Elo’a) in the height of heaven (Job 22:12). Furthermore, the word Elohim comes in the construct. Compare, Elohim Elohe yisra’el (God, the God of Israel) (Ps. 72:12). The word El (God) means mighty. The same is true of the term Shaddai (Almighty). Compare, Like the noise of great waters, like a mighty voice (Ezek. 1:24); and, and thy treasure shall be mighty (shaddai) (Job 22:25).

Note that the number one is the secret and the foundation of all numbers, and that two is the first of the even numbers and three the first of the odd numbers. Now from one point of view there are only nine numbers. However, from another perspective there are ten numbers. If the numbers one to nine are written in a circle and the last number is multiplied by each of the other numbers, we find that the ones are on the left and the tens, which look like ones, are on the right. Now when we come to the number five which is in the middle, we find the reverse; i.e., the tens become ones and the ones become tens. However, looked upon from another perspective, there are ten numbers without any additions, for one cannot begin to count one without ten. The number ten is thus like the number one. It is a general term for all the ones, i.e., the numbers from one through ten. The number ten includes them because they are the first numbers. It is also similar to the ones because it is the first of the numbers, in the same way that the ones are, because when we reach the number twenty we have two tens paralleling the number two. Similarly, thirty is like three and all the tens till ninety are like the nine ones. When the number one hundred is reached we once again come upon a number which is similar to one. When we reach nine hundred we once again have nine numbers similar to the nine ones. This is so until we reach the number one thousand which consists of ten hundreds. Also, the number one thousand is similar to the number one, and likewise the following numbers correspond to the other nine numbers until nine thousand. When we reach ten thousand the sum is concluded because we now have one myriad. The same applies until we reach ten myriads. The beginning of all the numbers is similar to the number one. Hence mathematicians say that all of the numbers are either fractions of ten or multiples of ten, or the result of adding ten to the ones, or a combination of these two. Now the ten numbers are the same as the fingers on the hand, five corresponding to five. Similarly, there are nine spheres which are in a constant glorious state. The tenth sphere, which is holy, is so called because its power is manifest throughout the throne of glory. It is the most powerful sphere and circles all the bodies. There are two middle digits when we count from one to ten, namely, the numbers five and six. Now the numbers alef (1), heh (5), vav (6), and yod (10) are the most glorious numerals. Any squared number that ends in one will always have the number one in its root. The same is true with its counterpart. Similarly, the number five will be found in the square of five and the number six will be found in the square of six. These four numbers always maintain their identity when squared; therein lies their superiority over all other numbers that are squared. Additionally, every number is potentially present in the number one. Similarly, the number one is found in all the actual numbers. Furthermore, the number one accomplishes on one side what the other numbers accomplish in two sides. Now behold the power of the number one. If you add its square to the square of its double you get five, a number whose cube equals its squares, for if you add its square to the square of its double it will equal its cube. In all the numbers preceding five the relationship of the cube to the sum of the two squared numbers will be the same as the relationship of that number to five. The reverse is the case with the numbers above five. The number six is equal to its parts. There is no other number in the order of the integers that equals its parts aside from this number. When the square of one is added to the square of the first of the odd numbers we get ten. Now if we bisect a circle with a line that is ten units long and a line is drawn across the circle a third of the way up, a triangle two of whose sides are equal may be drawn. The number representing the area of this triangle will equal the circumference of the circle. Similarly the rectangle formed in the circle. Now up to ten the value of the triangle to the circumference will be the same as the diameter is to ten. The reverse will be the case in the numbers above ten.

Now these four letters are very precious. They add up to twenty-two, the number of the letters in the Hebrew alphabet. Do not count the doubled letters twice, as they are the original letters with their horizontal bases straightened to form a line. The reason they have one name even though they are written differently is that they have one sound. The master of Hebrew grammar perceived that the letters have five sources. He classified half of the letters as root letters only, and half as root, prefix, or suffix letters. Now the second group of letters is more important than the first group. It is proper that a letter that is said often be one that is easy to pronounce. It is also fitting that the alef, heh, vav , and yod be easy to pronounce and have important meanings. These four letters are found in the vowels and are implied letters. These letters serve at times as consonants, at times as silent letters, and at times as paragogic letters. At times they drop out. At other times they are swallowed by a dagesh . Finally, at other times they interchange with each other.

Now there are four gutturals. They start with the ayin , which is followed by the chet . Do not consider all the letters that make up the name of a guttural in your definition of a guttural, as the additional letters are not made by the throat. It is best to refer to them as sounded with a pattach . Now the ayin and chet are very hard to sound. A person who is not accustomed to pronouncing them in his youth will not be able to sound them properly. Thus the gentiles cannot sound them. Hence only the alef and heh were chosen from among the gutturals to serve as ministering letters. Ministering letters were also chosen from among the palatals, i.e., gimel, yod, kaf, kof , as the palate is next to the throat. The yod and kaf were chosen from the palatals to serve as ministering letters because they are the easiest palatals to pronounce. The gimel and kof are therefore only used as root letters.

The letters dalet, tet, lamed, nun , and tav are linguals. Two letters, the dalet and the tet , were chosen from the linguals to serve only as root letters. The others serve both as root letters and as ministering letters. The letters zayin, samekh, shin, resh , and tzadi are dentals. They are all hard to pronounce. The shin is the easiest of the dentals to sound. Hence it was chosen as a ministering letter while the others were left to serve only as root letters. Therefore three letters were chosen from among the labials, namely, the bet, vav, mem , and peh , to serve as ministering letters. The peh was left to serve only as a root letter.

It is only right that the alphabet begin with a guttural, because the throat is the first organ in the framework of the human body to produce a sound. It does so from bottom to top. The alef comes before the heh because it is the easiest guttural to pronounce. Hence the alef heads all the other letters of the alphabet and is equivalent to the number one. It is fitting that the heh be the fifth number equivalent to the glorious number five. These two letters are the easiest to enunciate. Now since the first letter of the alphabet is a guttural the second letter in the alphabet was chosen from among the five labials, which are produced by the last of the body’s five organs of speech. Hence the bet follows the alef , the vav also follows the heh , and the peh the ayin . Now it was necessary to put in two letters between the bet and the heh . A palatal, the gimel , was chosen as the third letter and a lingual, the dalet , as the fourth letter. Hence a dental, namely, the zayin , follows the vav . The Hebrew grammarian now had to use the fourth of the implied letters for the tenth letter, which is equivalent to the number ten. He had already used the gutturals alef and heh whose great importance has previously been explained as the first and the fifth letters. He had similarly used the vav , which happens to be a very important and easily sounded labial. Now there are no root letters more easily pronounceable than the palatals. He chose from the palatals the yod and the kaf to serve as ministering letters. The more easily pronounceable of the two is the yod .

Four letters are fit to be implied letters. The alef is silent in all vowels because it is equivalent to the number one. We find the alef with the cholam in the word rosh (head); with the kamatz in roshim (heads); with the chirik in the word rishon (first); with the tzere in reshit (beginning of); with the shuruk in pura (boughs) in Shall lop the boughs (Is. 10:33); with the pattach in chattat (purification) in For purification and for sprinkling (Zech. 13:1); and with the segol in pele (wonders) in doing wonders (Ex. 16:11). It serves as a first person imperfect prefix in the masculine and in the feminine because it is the first letter of the alphabet. Since the alef is never sounded when it comes at the end of a word, it does not serve as the sign of the feminine. However, it occasionally takes the place of the heh , as in marah (bitter) in call me Marah (Ruth 1:20) and in gaveha (was exalted) in its stature was exalted (Ezek. 31:5). The alef is also found employed as a superfluous letter at the end of a word, as in ve-attikeiha (and the galleries thereof) (Ezek. 41:15) and he-halekhu (that went) in that went with him (Joshua 10:24). It is also found as a sounded superfluous letter at the beginning of a word, as in etmol (yesterday) (II Sam. 5:2) and ve-ezro’i (and my arm) (Job 31:22). It is similarly used in the middle of a word, as in ve-he’eznihu (shall become foul) in And the rivers shall become foul (Is. 19:6). The alef is also found unsounded at the end of a word, as in the word chet (sin) (Deut. 23:22). At times the silent alef is dropped, as in the word kes (throne) in the throne of the Lord (Ex. 17:14). At times it interchanges with a heh or a yod , as in ha-amon (the multitude) (Jer. 52:15), which is a variation of he-hamon (II Sam. 18:29); or tityammeru (shall ye revel) (Is. 61:6), which is a variation of yitammeru (Ps. 94:4). It is also found sounded with a vav , as in tomeru (say ye) in And say ye to Amasa (II Sam. 19:14).

Now these three letters are fit to serve as prefixes and suffixes. The letter yod , which is similar to the number one (the alef ), serves as a first person suffix both in the masculine and in the feminine. In the verbal forms we find shamarti (I have kept) (Ps. 17:4) and amarti (I have said) (Ex. 23:13); among the nouns we find shemi (my name) (Ex. 23:21). The yod is also employed as a third person masculine imperfect prefix, as the number ten is like the number one. In the feminine it is oppositely positioned and serves as a suffix, as in de’i (know), re’i (see) (I Sam. 28:17), and tizkeri (thou mayest remember) in that thou mayest remember (Ezek. 16:63). This yod also shows relationship because as a numeral it is similar to the number one. The yod is a sign of the plural construct connected to the third person, as in yede (hands of) in The hands of women full of compassion (Lam. 4:10) and yadai (my hands) in even My hands have stretched out the heavens (Is. 45:12) because the number ten includes all numbers in it. The yod is encountered as a silent letter when it follows a chirik , as in ragli (my foot) (Ps. 26:10); a tzere , as in ragle (the feet of) in He will keep the feet of his holy ones (I Sam. 2:9); or a kamatz , as in yadav (his hands) and raglav (his feet). The yod is found in place of a heh (it is also found in place of a vav ), as in hoyah (is) (Ex. 9:3), which is a variation of the word hovah (wouldest be) in and thou wouldest be their king (Nehemiah 6:6). The yod takes the place of a heh in the word yechesayun (take refuge) (Ps. 36:8), which comes from the root chet, samekh, heh . It takes the place of an alef in yisharti (to be right) in all precepts…all things to be right (Ps. 119:128). The yod is found as a superfluous letter in the words yitzhar (oil) (Num. 18:12), ha-yoshevi (that art enthroned) (Ps. 123:1), and rabbati (great) (Lam. 1:1). The heh is also used to indicate the presence of a thing, for this is its meaning in he lakehem zera (Lo, here is seed for you) (Gen. 47:23). The heh is also sometimes used to introduce a question, as in ha-bemachanim (whether in camps) (Num. 13:19), and ha-niheyeh (whether there hath been) (Deut. 4:32); or as the sign of the definite article, as in ha-eved ha-ivri (the Hebrew servant) (Gen. 39:17) and ha-anashim (the men) (Gen. 19:5). The heh suffixed to a verb indicates a third person feminine perfect. It is similarly used with nouns. The masculine form, on the other hand, was left without a sign. Compare the word amar and the word amerah in saith Koheleth (Eccles. 7:27). The heh is also used as a sign of the feminine when the imperfect is combined with the pronoun, as in eshmerenah (I will watch her), yishmerennah (he will watch her), nishmerennah (we will watch her), tishmerennah (you will watch her), yishmeruha (they will watch her), shemarnuha (we watched her), and shimruha (watch her). The heh serves as the sign of the feminine noun, compare, na’arah be-tulah (a damsel that is a virgin) (Deut. 22:28). The heh is appended to the hifil and also to the hitpa’el conjugations. The heh is also at times dropped, as in the word mazzeh (what is that) in What is that in thy hand (Ex. 4:2). It is similar to the yod of etzarekha (I formed thee) in Before I formed thee (Jer. 1:4), and it is like the alef of va-abbedkha (and I have destroyed thee) in and I have destroyed thee, O covering cherub (Ezek. 28:16). It is also superfluously appended to the end of a verb, as in eshme’ah (I will hear), or a noun as in laylah (night). It is silent when following the kamatz, tzere, segol, cholam , or shuruk . Compare the words asah (made) and boneh (doth build) in the Lord doth build up Jerusalem (Ps. 147:2); boneh (build) in And the house which I build (II Chron. 2:4); pera’oh (let them loose) in for Aaron had let them loose (Ex. 32:25), also shelomoh (Solomon) and yikrechu (they shall not make baldness) (Lev. 21:5).

The vav is used as a connective and is in such instances placed in front of the word because the vav sound is made by connecting the lips. The vav is used as a connective in the phrases avraham ve-yitzchak (Abraham and Isaac) (Gen. 48:16) and in mi fa’al ve-asah (who hath wrought and done it) (Is. 41:4). The vav is also employed as a masculine and feminine plural perfect suffix. It is also used as a masculine imperfect suffix. It is similarly employed at times as a feminine imperfect suffix, as in im timtze’u (if ye find) (Cant. 5:8) and im ta’iru (that ye awaken not (Cant., 7:2). The vav is found as a silent letter when employed with the shuruk and cholam vowels. It is used as a masculine pronominal suffix with words in the perfect, as in shemaro (he watched him); with a noun, as in yado (his hand), and with a verb in the imperfect, as in yirdefo (will pursue him). It is vocalized with a shuruk following a heh , or a nun with a dagesh , as in yishmerehu (preserve him) (Ps. 41:3) or yishmerennu be’alav (its owner hath…kept it in) (Ex. 21:36), because the heh is used as a feminine suffix. The vav is also used as a sign of the plural in verbs in the perfect and imperfect.

I have shown that these four letters are implied letters. Therefore the proper names that are constructed from these four glorious letters are glorious names. Now the first of these divine names is only found here. It is not encountered elsewhere in Scripture. We know that when Moses spoke to Pharaoh he enunciated God’s name as written. He did not employ any substitute. Moses acted thus because he was holy. However, the ancients were forced to use a substitute name when referring to God. The meaning of and this is My memorial is the same as this is My name , as our text employs two words with one meaning. Our reading of the divine name as Elohim whenever it is connected to Adonai , the meaning of which is, He is Lord, is proof of the above. This word comes in the plural out of deference to God in the same way that Elohim does. Hence if someone addresses the Lord in the same way that he addresses a person and says Adoni (my Lord), as in adoni sha’al (My lord asked) (Gen. 44:19), he errs.

I will now explain the meaning. Know that there are three worlds. One of them, the lower world, consists of objects that are on various levels of importance. However, they can be classified in three groups. The first is the metals, which number seven and correspond to the seven stars. At a higher level come the plants, which have many levels of value. Above them come living things, which have many levels of importance. Man alone is on the highest level in this lower world. Change befalls him in his body. Also his soul changes with his thoughts. Similarly, change befalls his occupation and his affairs. The wise men have compared the genera which is the group that endures although the individuals which make it up perish. The wise men have compared the intransient species to the shadow of a tree upon the ever-running water.

The next world is the middle world. It too contains objects that are on various levels of importance. The five ministering stars are very important, as they are self-sufficient and do not die or diminish. Neither do their movements change, enlarge, or shrink. They do not ascend or descend. Howbeit, they do change greatly according to the arrangement. At times a given star is seen in the line of the zodiac; at other times it is seen at a greater or nearer distance to the left, or at a greater or nearer distance to the right. Sometimes it ascends in its epicycle, at other times in its large sphere, for the center of the latter is far from the center of the earth. Sometimes its sphere ascends or descends. At other times it runs. Sometimes it tarries. At other times it stands in its place. Sometimes it goes backwards. All of this is vis-à-vis the earth. Sometimes it is seen. At other times it is hidden. Sometimes it is in the east, at other times in the west. Its relation to its companion, and also to the hosts of heaven above and to the moon below, is indeterminately forever changing because it is sometimes in conjunction with one of the seven fixed stars. Now there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions in each one of the three hundred and sixty degrees. It is due to these irregular movements that different things happen to man’s body and certainly to his fortune in this lower world. However, these stars themselves do not change. The moon is therefore on a lower level than they, because whatever happens to the stars happens to the moon, and even more. They have two spheres, neither of which has the earth as its center. Furthermore, the moon’s movement in its epicycle is opposite that of the great sphere. Additionally, the moon by herself has no light. Her light comes from the sun. This can be seen from the fact that when the moon is in conjunction with the sun in the head or tail of the dragon during the day, the sun cannot be seen, and if it faces the sun in one of the above-noted places at night the moon is invisible.

Now the stars that make up the sphere of the constellations are a level above the “ministers.” They are fixed in one sphere and they do not move as the ministers do. Their distances and relationship to each other do not change. They have one motion; it neither increases nor decreases. Their relationship to the earth is always the same. They appear different according to the place on earth where they are seen and the movement of the sun. The highest world is the world of the holy angels who are incorporeal and, unlike the souls of men, do not inhabit bodies. Their importance is far and above the understanding of their insignificant counterparts. This entire world is glorious and unchanging. There is no change in its arrangement. This world is not self-sufficient but its existence is dependent upon God the glorious. Man’s soul is of this same kind. It receives power from above in accordance to the arrangement of the ministers, that is, the arrangement of each “minister” vis-à-vis the great hosts at the time of a person’s birth. If the soul grows wise it will share the secrets of the angels and will be able to receive great power from an upper power that received it from the light of the angels. The person will then cleave to God the glorious. This is precisely what Jacob meant when he vowed, then shall the Lord be my God (Gen. 28:21). Jacob vowed that he would dedicate his entire life to cleave unto God to the fullest of his might. Jacob therefore said, Put away the strange gods that are among you (Gen. 35:2). Jacob did not utter these words till this point, for it was only now that he was going to serve God according to his vow. So too, Jethro, who said, Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods . (Ex. 18:11). Jethro was a very wise man. Proof of the latter is, And they asked each other of their welfare (Ex. 18:7). Additionally, Scripture states, and bowed down ( Ibid. ), which implies that Jethro did not stand in awe of Moses.

When Adam realized that he would die he sired a son so that the human kind would be preserved. He received the power to preserve the human genus. Hence Eve exclaimed, I have gotten a man with the help of God (Gen. 4:1). Each one of the sons of the prophets used to isolate himself in the hope of being inspired from on high according to his ability. Now it is via this name that new signs and wonders come into this world. When this name was told to Pharaoh he asked for signs and wonders. Therefore this name is not found in the book of Koheleth, as this book speaks of things concerning which nothing can be added nor anything taken away (Eccles. 3:4). It deals with those things concerning which there is nothing new under the sun (Eccles. 1:9). It deals with those things which are based on the wisdom that comes from on high.
GO, AND GATHER. Scripture reads, the God of Abraham because God made a covenant with Abraham to give him the land of Canaan.
[I HAVE SURELY REMEMBERED YOU.] The meaning of pakod (remembered) is that the time of their visitation had come.

AND I HAVE SAID. I have previously said to your fathers that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt , the reference being to and afterward shall they come out with great substance (Gen. 15:14), and to and I will also surely bring thee up again (Gen. 46:4). Or its meaning is, I have now decreed that this shall come to pass, as in Thou shalt also decree a thing (Job 22:28).

AND THEY SHALL HEARKEN. When the word shama (heard) is followed by a lamed or bet its meaning is not to hear a voice but rather to hear the message which a voice carries. The yod in the word ha-ivriyyim (the Hebrews) has a dagesh for euphonic purposes. It is there to emphasize the yod genitive. The yod in ha-ivrim (the Hebrews) that follows the resh with a chirik beneath it is, in accordance with Hebrew grammar, the sign of the plural.

HATH MET WITH US. Nikrah (hath met) means the same whether spelled with a heh or an alef . Compare, nikro nikreti (as I happened by chance) (II Sam. 1:6). I will now explain the meaning of nikrah . Its meaning is, lest he fall upon us (Ex. 5:3).
AND I KNOW THAT THE KING OF EGYPT WILL NOT GIVE YOU. Leave. Or the meaning of yitten (give you) is, let, as in Therefore suffered I thee not (netatikha) to touch her (Gen. 20:6).
[EXCEPT BY A MIGHTY HAND.] Neither will he let you go because of his mighty hand. However, Saadiah explains it to mean: neither will he let you go if he is struck once with a mighty hand.
AND I WILL PUT FORTH MY HAND. Against his hand.

AND I WILL GIVE. The Egyptians’ appeasing of the Israelites by imploring them to ask for jewels and raiments (which is the meaning of va-yashilum ) was also a great wonder. This is the opposite of the behavior of the world’s inhabitants.
[EMPTY.] The mem of rekam (empty) is superfluous. The word rekam is used in the plural as in our verse. It is also used as a feminine in Go not empty (Ruth 3:17). The word chinnam is similar.

BUT EVERY WOMEN SHALL ASK. Now elsewhere it is written with regard to both males and females, and let them ask (Ex. 11:2). Scripture mentions females here because women are more in the habit of asking their neighbors for jewelry of gold and silver to put on the necks of their sons and daughters. They are likewise in the habit of asking for ear rings, nose rings, bracelets, crescents, and anklets. This is the contemporary custom in Moslem countries. However, the inhabitants of the land of the uncircumcised do not act in this manner. Scripture similarly speaks of a sorceress, as women are more involved in witchcraft than men.

AND OF HER THAT SOJOURNETH IN HER HOUSE. For the Israelites owned land.Some complain and say that our ancestors were thieves. Can’t these murmurers see that this was a command from on high? There is no sense in asking why? God created everything. He gives riches to whom He desires to give it, and when He wishes to, He takes the very same riches away. There is no evil in this, as everything is His.

AND YE SHALL SPOIL. Ve-nitzaltem (and ye shall despoil) is like ve-dibbartem (and speak ye) (Num. 20:8), for it is possible that its form is that of the nifal conjugation. Compare, ve-niggaftem (and ye shall be smitten) (Lev. 26:17).

AND MOSES ANSWERED. God indicated to Moses that the elders would believe in him. However, He did not mention this explicitly. And they shall hearken to thy voice (Ex. 3:18) relates only to behavior and not to inner belief.

AND THE LORD SAID. This sign was not given to Moses so that he would believe, because He had already given him the sign of the bush. God performed this sign for Moses so that Moses would imitate it before the children of Israel. It is therefore written, that they may believe (v. 5), which means, thus shall you do before them. God gave Moses a sign via an object that was always with him, the staff, Moses’ walking stick, as is the custom with elders. Moses would not appear as a shepherd before Pharaoh.

AND HE SAID. Those versed in the sciences ask, how is this possible? They were forced to conclude that it was to remove the dryness. However, all their words are empty wind, as we are dealing with a wondrous event, one that did not occur according to the laws of nature.

Yefet says that this wonder was a hint, as Pharaoh was at first soft like a staff and then turned into a serpent. It is written, Pharaoh King of Egypt, The great serpent (Ezek. 29:3). At the end he ended up the way he started; he was like one that never existed.

AND THE LORD SAID. The first sign was performed upon the staff that was found in Moses’ hand. The second one was executed on Moses’ very hand. Yefet says that his hand became leprous because he suspected that the Israelites would not believe him. However, if this were the case, this should have been the first sign. Rabbi Joshua says that this was a hint about Israel, who at first were free and then God plagued them with Egyptian bondage, and that God would eventually heal them and that they would be free once again.

AND THE LORD SAID. Saadiah Gaon says that chek (bosom) refers to the sleeve of the arm. Similarly u-ve-cheko yissa (and carrieth them in his bosom) (Is. 40:11) and sa’ehu ve-chekekha (carry them in thy bosom) (Num. 11:12). Others say that it refers to a garment that lies close to the chest.

AND IT SHALL COME TO PASS. We know that God knew whether they would believe or not. Scripture, however, speaks with regard to Moses, viz., if there will be some Israelites who will not believe the first sign, then they will believe the latter sign ( ha’ot ha-acharon ). Scripture speaks of the voice of the sign . Now a sign has no voice. The Torah, however, speaks in the language of man, as it does in Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Prov. 18:21). Scripture speaks of the latter sign even though there were three signs, because God now showed only two signs to Moses, as He was yet to perform the third sign.

AND IT SHALL COME TO PASS. If there shall still be a few Israelites that will not believe the last sign, then you will show them the third sign and they shall believe. Indeed, it is written, and (Moses) did the signs in the sight of the people (v. 30). This third sign, namely, and the water…shall become blood upon the dry land was part of the first of the ten plagues which were destined to come.

AND MOSES SAID. All the commentaries agree that bi (oh) is to be taken as a supplicatory expression. However, Rabbi Judah Ha-Levi says that bi is an abridgement. It is short for bi ani adoni he-avon (Upon me, my lord, upon me be the iniquity) (I Sam. 25:24), that is, punish me as you wish but relieve me of this task and do not send me. Similarly bi adoni yedabber na avdekha davar (oh my lord, let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word in my lord’s ears) (Gen. 44:18). Its meaning is, do to me as you wish but allow me to speak.

A MAN OF WORDS. A person who knows how to speak elegantly, that is, a person who does not halt or stutter or have difficulty in enunciating certain letters. It is the custom of the Hebrews when they went to compare two or three things to add the word gam (also) to the first object, as in Rule over us, also you, also your son and also your son’s son (Jud. 8:22).

[HERETOFORE.] The explanation of the word shilshom (third day) is as follows. The word temol (yesterday) refers to the day before the one in which the person is speaking. Shilshom thus refers to the third day from which the person is speaking. The mem in shilshom is the mem of the plural as it refers to today and yesterday, even though its shin is not vocalized with a kamatz as the rules of grammar require. On the other hand, it is possible that the mem is appended at the end of the word as it is to the beginning of the word. Compare, the word mishlosh (three) in And it came to pass about three months after (Gen. 38:24).

NOR SINCE THOU HAST SPOKEN. Me-az dabberkha (since thou hast spoken) is to be rendered, from the time that thou hast spoken. Me-az (since) in For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in Thy name (Ex. 5:23) is similar, as the slowness of his speech was not removed but remained as it was. The one who says that Moses forgot Egyptian is incorrect, because Moses mentioned two things, viz., slowness of speech and slowness of tongue. Furthermore, we can learn from God’s answer, Who hath made man’s mouth? or who maketh a man dumb? that Moses was not referring to the Egyptian language. The upshot of this is that Moses was born with slowness of speech; i.e., he could not pronounce the labials or all of the linguals. However, he was able to pronounce some of them with difficulty. This is the meaning of, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak ; i.e., God told Moses that He would teach him to speak with words that do not contain letters that he had difficulty enunciating.

AND THE LORD SAID. We find dumb corresponding to the making of the mouth, blind corresponding to seeing , while the word deaf stands by itself; it has no counterpart. However, in reality the word pike’ach (seeing) corresponds both to blind and to deaf, as it is written, pako’ach oznayim (opening the ears) (Is. 42:20); li-feko’ach enayim ivrot (to open the blind eyes) (Is. 42:7).
Behold, God did not now promise Moses that He would remove the slowness of his tongue. He only promised to teach him what to speak.

AND HE SAID. I have already explained that the word na (I pray) always means now in Scripture. See, Speak now (na) in the ears of the people (Ex. 11:2); Hear now (na), O Joshua the high priest (Zech. 3:8); Let this man, now (na) be put to death (Jer. 38:4); Woe now (na) unto us! for we have sinned (Lam. 5:16).

WHOM THOU WILT SEND. The word asher (whom) has been omitted. Our verse is to be read as if written be-yad asher tishlach . Im levavam shalem (whose heart is whole) (II Chron. 16:9) is similar. Its meaning is, send this message by the hand of Aaron my brother who is a man of words , for he is not of slow speech and he is in the habit of prophesying to Israel. Indeed, it is written in the book of Ezekiel that God sent a prophet to Israel before he sent our master Moses. Scripture also states, And the Lord said to Aaron: Go into the wilderness to meet Moses (Ex. 4:27). Furthermore, since Aaron was older than Moses, he might be angry if Moses was appointed God’s messenger to Pharaoh. It is for this reason that God told Moses, and when he (Aaron) seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart (Ex. 4:14). Now Moses did not refuse to go.

What happened was that Moses first replied, I am not a man of words (v. 10), and it is difficult for one who is slow of speech to speak before the king. Moses thought that God would miraculously remove his slowness of speech. However, when God answered him, and (I) will teach thee what thou shalt speak (v. 12), Moses knew that his slowness of speech would not be removed. Moses thus wondered why God did not send Aaron to Pharaoh. It is for this reason that he said, send, I pray Thee, by the hand of him whom Thou wilt send . All of this can be clearly derived from God’s answer, Is not Aaron thy brother… (v. 14).

AND THE ANGER OF THE LORD WAS KINDLED. Heaven forbid that this be the meaning of the verse, that the Lord…sought to kill him (v. 24), as he should have killed him now when he refused to go, not when he went, as others have interpreted. Why kill him when he went? Our case cannot be compared to that of Balaam. Similarly, the incident with Jacob is different. Should someone argue, where do we find a case where God’s anger did not cause harm, we will show him, And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them (Num. 12:9), yet no harm befell Aaron.Scripture refers to Aaron as the Levite , for this is the way the Levite prophet was known in Israel since there were others who bore this name. Now Aaron’s appointment as spokesman did not entail Moses’ demotion. On the contrary, Moses’ status was thereby elevated. Aaron was merely an instrument, similar to the mouth which brings forth the words of the invisible soul which, like the angels, cannot be seen because they are incorporeal. Moses’ station was thus similar to the station of an angel. This is the meaning of And thou shalt be to him in Elohim’s (God’s) stead (v. 16). Now Elohim in Scripture does not refer to anything but God the glorious or His holy angels or the holy ones below who execute God’s justice in the world. Whenever Scripture refers to an idol by the term elohim it does so in keeping with the beliefs of its worshippers. It is similar to unto the prophet Hananiah (Jer. 28:5).

AND…THIS ROD. Scripture refers to the signs because the rod changed into a serpent before all of Israel and into a serpent before Pharaoh. The rod was also used to strike the Nile, to bring up frogs, to produce gnats, to bring down hail, to bring locusts, and to cause darkness.

AND MOSES WENT…JETHER. Jether and Jethro are one and the same. Similarly, Geshem (Neh. 6:2) and Gashmu (Neh. 6:6) are one and the same, as are Salmah (Ruth 4:20) and Salmon (Ruth 4:21). Moses told Jethro that he was going to see his brethren. He did not reveal the secret to him.

AND THE LORD SAID. The Torah is not in chronological order. The meaning of and the Lord said is, and the Lord had said. Similarly, And out of the ground made the Lord to grow (Gen. 2:9) and many other such instances. Now when Moses was handing over Jethro’s sheep to Jethro, God assured him that he could go to Egypt without trepidation because Pharaoh and his servants who knew about the incident of the Egyptian were dead. This is the meaning of that the king of Egypt died (Ex. 2:23); as long as Pharaoh lived it was improper for Moses to be a messenger to him.

AND MOSES TOOK. We do not know whether Gershom was born at the time that Moses was a young man, when he fled to Midian, or during his old age. Do not rely on The History of Moses , as everything written in it is nonsense. Moses’ second son, namely, Eliezer, was born now, at the time that Moses started to prophesy. Moses planned to bring his wife and sons to Egypt so that they could leave Egypt together with all of Israel. However, this was not a good idea; he was going to bring the Israelites out of Egypt and they would see that he came with his wife and children to live there. Do not be surprised that a prophet should incorrectly assess practical events, for indeed we find that David asked Nathan the prophet whether is was proper for him to build a temple to the Lord. Nathan then answered him, All that is in thy heart do, for the Lord is with thee . However, in a prophetic vision of the night, Nathan was told to inform David that he should not build the temple.The elders were forced to translate upon an ass as upon the man carrier, because it is demeaning that the wife of the prophet and her two sons should ride on one ass. Yefet says that ass is used as a collective noun, as in And I have an ox and an ass (Gen. 32:6). However, Yefet is incorrect. This is not the place to use collective nouns. The term thus must be taken literally. Now the asses in Egypt are dearer and more precious than the mules. There is nothing to wonder about if his son Gershom rode behind his mother. Perhaps he was small and Eliezer was in her bosom for he was not yet circumcised.

[AND HE RETURNED TO THE LAND OF EGYPT.] Its meaning is that only Moses himself returned. When God met Moses (v. 24) Eliezer was circumcised (v. 25). When Eliezer was healed, Zipporah and her children returned to her father. Moses left them and went on to Egypt.

Scripture refers to the staff as the rod of God because of the sign that was performed with it. The rod of God is the same as the rod of Moses and the rod of Aaron. It was in his hand when he did the signs. Now that the rod of God is mentioned Scripture backtracks and relates that God told Moses all the wonders that he was destined to do in Egypt. He mentioned to Moses the sign that would bring Israel out of Egypt, namely, the plague of the first-born.

[AND IT CAME TO PASS ON THE WAY AT THE LODGING-PLACE.] This should have been connected to And Moses took his wife and his sons (v. 20). There are many such cases in the Pentateuch, an example being, he shall make restitution (Ex. 22:2). The latter is connected to he shall pay five oxen for an ox (Ex. 21:37).

AND THE LORD SAID. This was told to Moses in Midian. God informed Moses that He would harden Pharaoh’s heart and that Pharaoh would not let them go despite all of the wonders, including the last one, that He would show them.

AND THOU SHALT SAY. The meaning of Israel is My son, My first-born is: the ancestors of this nation were the first to serve Me. I therefore take pity on this nation as a father pities a son who serves him. You took him for a perpetual slave. I will therefore kill your first-born son.

AND I HAVE SAID UNTO THEE. Behold, I have told you time and time again to let My son go, that he may serve Me by offering sacrifices to Me, and thou hast refused to let him go. I will therefore punish thee. The ignorant say that these words are directed at Moses. The latter is sheer madness. Furthermore, Eliezer was not Moses’ first-born.

AND IT CAME TO PASS ON THE WAY. They had a tradition that a child should not be circumcised on the eighth day if he was sick, or while traveling when it was not possible for his guardian to tarry and circumcise him. Now because Moses could not tarry in carrying out God’s mission he concluded that he should not circumcise his son, because the child would be in danger if he were taken along. God therefore sent an angel to tell Moses to put his decision aside and to circumcise the lad. The child would then remain with his mother until healed and Moses would continue on by himself.

[THAT THE LORD MET HIM.] Its meaning is that God sent an illness upon Moses because it did not occur to him. This then is the meaning of and sought to slay him : God sought to slay Moses if he would not circumcise his son. Now because Moses was seized with trembling he could not circumcise his son. Zipporah circumcised him, for Moses revealed this secret to her. Do not be surprised that it is written, That the Lord met him ; the reference is to an angel of the Lord. And the Lord went before them (Ex. 13:21) is similar, and there it is written, And the angel of God…removed (Ex. 14:19). However, Rabbi Samuel ben Hofni says: Perish the thought that God would seek to slay Moses who was on God’s mission to redeem His people. It was rather Eliezer whom the Lord sought to slay, and it is to Eliezer that the third person pronominal suffixes of va-yifgeshehu (met him) and hamito (slay him) refer. Scripture then goes on to explain that the reference is to Eliezer. Scripture therefore states, and cut off the foreskin of her son . He is not at first mentioned because he did not as yet have a name. And it came to pass, when she travailed, that one put out a hand (Gen. 38:28) is similar.

THEN ZIPPORAH TOOK A FLINT. A sharp instrument. Compare, Make thee knives of flint (Josh. 5:2) which refers to sharp knives. Yea, thou turnest back the flint (tzur) of his sword (Ps. 89:44) is similar.

[AND CAST IT AT HIS FEET.] In my opinion the reference is to Moses’ feet. Our verse is like and when He seeth the blood upon the lintel, and upon the side-posts, the Lord…will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to destroy you (Ex. 12:23). Therefore He let him , that is, Moses, alone; his illness and shivering ceased. However, Rabbi Samuel says that his feet refers to Eliezer’s feet, and similarly He let him alone . This being the case we can refute him by asking, “If the illness befell Eliezer how could Zipporah circumcise him, thereby adding pain to his pain?”
[A BRIDEGROOM OF BLOOD.] It is the custom of women to refer to a child as a bridegroom when he is circumcised.
[BLOOD.] Its meaning is, surely thou art a man of blood to me , for because of you my husband will die.

SO HE LET HIM ALONE. The word damim (blood) in Hebrew is used in two ways. One way is to indicate bloodshed, as in because thou art a man of blood to me (II Sam. 16:8). The person who says that damim refers to life is giving the word a meaning that it does not have. The second way is as a plural referring to actual blood, as in be-damayikh chayi (in thy blood live) (Ezek. 16:6). Now when Zipporah saw that the illness left Moses she exclaimed, you my son are not a bridegroom of blood, blood referring to death, but you are a bridegroom wallowing in the blood of circumcision. The word mulot (circumcision) is a noun. It is in the plural because of damim (blood).

AND THE LORD SAID TO AARON. Aaron did not prophesy; there was no need for him to do so as Moses was the messenger sent to Pharaoh. However, prior to this Aaron had been sent as messenger to the male Israelites, and Miriam to the females. The prophet therefore says, And I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam (Micah 6:4).
IN THE MOUNTAIN OF GOD. The reference is to Mount Horeb.
AND MOSES TOLD. God sent Moses to Israel first.
AND ALL THE SIGNS WHEREWITH HE HAD CHARGED HIM. To first perform before Israel and then to perform other signs before Pharaoh.
AND MOSES AND AARON WENT. The elders are the counselors in each generation, as Moses and Aaron could not possibly speak to six hundred thousand men. It was rather the elders who spoke to them.
AND AARON SPOKE. For he was Moses’ mouthpiece. Moses therefore never spoke to Israel except through Aaron. When Aaron died his son Eleazar took his place and similarly became Moses’ mouthpiece.
AND THE PEOPLE BELIEVED. After they heard that the Lord had remembered his people. The end of the time period that had been told to Abraham had come.
THEIR AFFLICTION. Onyam comes from the same root as inuy (affliction).

THEN THEY BOWED. Va-yikkedu (then they bowed) comes from a double root. It is like the word kodkod (skull). Va-yikkedu follows the paradigm of va-yittemu (were ended) in so the days of weeping in the mourning of Moses were ended (Deut. 34:8) and yiddemu (they are still) in they are as still as stone (Ex. 16:16). If only those who say that these words come from roots that begin with a nun would be as still as stone . In order to explain the paradigm they add roots that are nonexistent in the holy tongue. Can they not see that the word redu (get you down) (Gen. 42:2) follows the paradigm of benu (build ye) in Build ye (lakhem) houses (Jer. 29:5) although they are two different roots. The correct thing is to do everything in our power not to multiply roots because of paradigms.
AND AFTERWARD. After Aaron did the signs the two of them came to Pharaoh and the two of them spoke. For the Lord had promised them, and I will be with thy mouth , and with his mouth (Ex. 4:15).

AND SAID…THUS SAITH THE LORD, THE GOD OF ISRAEL. Pharaoh had never before heard this name. Moses therefore added the God of Israel , the meaning of which is, the people of Israel and not only the patriarch Jacob.

THAT THEY MAY HOLD A FEAST ( VE-YACHOGU ) UNTO ME IN THE WILDERNESS. That they may sacrifice unto me. Compare, bind the offering (chag) to the horns of the altar with cords , and chaggim (offerings) in Let the offerings come round (Is. 29:1).
AND PHARAOH SAID: WHO IS THE LORD, THAT I SHOULD HEARKEN UNTO HIS VOICE. He asked, “Who is the Lord that he is God?” We learn this from Moses’ answer to Pharaoh, which follows.

AND THEY SAID. This name refers to the God of the Hebrews. The Hebrews were a group whom the Egyptians were familiar with. The term Hebrew refers to Abraham, who is called the Hebrew. It likewise refers to Abraham’s son Isaac and to Jacob and his sons, as I will explain when I comment on the verse if thou buy a Hebrew servant (Ex. 21:2).

AND THEY SAID. The word nikra (hath met) is similar to nikro nikreti (as I happened by chance) in As I happened by chance upon mount Gilboa (II Sam. 1:6). It means met. He explained to Pharaoh why they are obligated to offer sacrifices, i.e., lest a pestilence or sword come upon us.

LEST HE FALL UPON US. Upon us includes us Israelites, also you, Pharaoh, and all the Egyptians. When Pharaoh saw that swarms of animals came and devoured many Egyptians, as it is written, He sent among them swarms of animals, which devoured them (Ps. 78:45), he said, Go ye, sacrifice to your God in the land (Ex. 8:21). However, Moses answered him, it is not meet so to do in the land (Ps. 8:22). On the contrary, they would go a distance of three days’ journey into the wilderness (Ps. 8:23). The latter is the distance between Egypt and Mount Sinai for one who takes a straight path. It was there that the Israelites offered sacrifices, as it is written, ye shall serve God upon this mountain (Ex. 3:12). It is furthermore written, and Moses builded an altar under the mount (Ex. 24:4). Also, the altar that Moses built after Amalek was defeated was erected on Mount Sinai, as it is written, and (Israel) encamped in Rephidim (Ex. 17:1), and it is there written, Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb (Ex. 17:6). When the locusts came Pharaoh gave some of the Israelites permission to go and sacrifice (Ex. 10:11). After the plague of darkness Pharaoh gave them all permission to go, with the exception that their cattle were to remain (Ex. 11:24). Now when they saw that a plague came and struck their first-born, Moses’ words, lest he fall upon us with pestilence , became clear. They therefore said, We are all dead men (Ex. 12:33). The Egyptians then chased them out (Ex. 12:39) to go and sacrifice. They also let them have what they asked for (Ex. 12:36).

AND THE KING OF EGYPT SAID. The word tafri’u (ye cause to break loose) means ye cause to disrupt. Yifra (cast off restraint) in When there is no vision, the people cast off restraint (yifra) (Prov. 29:18) is similar. Pharaoh included Moses and Aaron in get you unto your burdens , for Moses and Aaron represented all of Israel. Your burdens does not mean your affairs. And will ye make them rest from their burdens (v. 5) proves the aforementioned.

AND PHARAOH SAID. Yefet says that the meaning of the people of the land are now many is, we are not concerned if pestilence or sword befalls them, for those who toil are many. However, according to my opinion its meaning is, you are seeking to cause a great amount of work to cease.
AND THE SAME DAY PHARAOH COMMANDED. The taskmasters were Egyptian and the officers of the people were Israelites.
YE SHALL NO MORE GIVE. Tosifun (ye shall more) is spelled with an alef . However, it is usually spelled with a vav . Both of these letters interchange with the yod .
[STRAW.] It is customary for those who build with soil to mix it with straw or chaff so that it will last.

TO MAKE BRICK. Lilbon (to make brick) comes from the same root as levenah (brick). A brick structure is stronger than a stone structure, because a structure made out of soil will be damaged by water and a stone structure will be harmed by fire. It is similarly written, And they had brick for stone , and slime had they for mortar (Gen. 11:3). Note, there are nouns that are vocalized with a tzere , such as the word sefer (book), or a segol , i.e., tzedek (righteousness), whose status does not change at an etnach or at the end of a verse. The word teven (straw) falls into this category. We not know the reason for the this; however, such is the case.
AND GATHER. Ve-kosheshu (and gather) comes from the same root as kash (stubble). comes from a double root.
AND THE TALE. Matkonet means tale. It refers to a specified amount.

LET HEAVIER WORK BE LAID. Saadiah Gaon says that al yishu (let them not regard) is like al yishanu (let them not rely) with the nun omitted, as it is in the word tet (to put) in I begin to put the dread of thee (Deut. 2:25). Pay no attention nor listen to the dreamer who says that the root of tet is tat . Because he found Scripture employing the word tattah (you put) in My enemies you put to flight before me (II Sam. 22:41), he thought that tattah is like shattah (thou hast set) in Thou hast set our iniquities before Thee (Ps. 90:8). Now he cannot deny that the second tav in the word tattah indicates the second person and the tav of the root is swallowed in the dagesh , even though the tav should receive a dagesh like the tav in ve-hishbatti (and I will cause to cease) in and I will cause evil beasts to cease out of the land (Lev. 26:6). Since this is the case it is better for the nun to be swallowed as it is swallowed by the tav in the word va-amitto (and his truth) (Gen. 24:27), for the word amitto should have been written aminto and the word bat (daughter), benat and the word tet, tenet . The missing first nun of the word tattah in tattah li is similar to the missing yod in rad (spent) in the day was far spent (Jud. 19:11) and to the missing nun in the word ga (touch) in Touch the mountains, that they may smoke (Ps. 144:5). However, in my opinion the word yishu (regard) means slack off, as Pharaoh said, for they are idle (nirpim) (v. 8). Yishu is similar to hasha (let go) in Let go of me (Ps. 39:14) and she’u (let go) in Let go of me (Is. 22:4), and to hasha (weaken) in And weaken their eyes (Is. 6:10), for when the eyes weaken they grow dim. Tishenah (shall be closed) in And the eyes of them that see shall be closed (Is. 32:3) is similar.
[LYING WORDS.] Its meaning is, because of the lying words that Moses and Aaron assure them with.
WENT OUT. Of the king’s palace to the people who were working.
GO YOURSELVES, GET YOU STRAW WHERE YE CAN FIND IT. Close by or far off.
FOR NOUGHT OF YOUR WORK SHALL BE DIMINISHED. Nigra (diminished) is a participle. It is therefore vocalized with a kamatz as is the rule.
WERE SCATTERED. Va-yafetz (were scattered) is a transitive verb. Pharaoh, who caused them to scatter, is the subject.
FOR STRAW. In place of straw. Compare, la-chomer (for mortar) in and slime had they for mortar (Gen. 11:3).
AND THE TASKMASTERS WERE URGENT. Atzim (urgent) is a transitive verb. It is like the word shav (returned) and the word mash (moved), which is sometimes found transitive and at times intransitive.
[SAYING.] Its meaning is, saying to them..
DAILY. The phrase devar yom be-yomo (daily) is similar to And from one sabbath to another (Is. 66:23).
AND THE OFFICERS…OVER THEM. Over the Israelites.

[BOTH YESTERDAY AND TO-DAY.] I have previously explained the use of the additional gam (both). Now, both yesterday refers to the day that Moses did the signs before the eyes of the people and they consequently were not occupied with their work. To-day refers to the day that Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh. And thus it is written, And the same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people (v. 6).
WHEREFORE DEALEST THOU THUS WITH THY SERVANTS? It was never your practice to do this.

BUT THE FAULT IS IN THINE OWN PEOPLE. The word ve-chatat (but the fault is) is a verb in the perfect. However, the vav changes it into an imperfect in accordance with the rules of grammar. The word is similar to ve-chate’ah . Now when the alef was silenced, as it is in the word chata , it was not possible to place a heh after the alef . They therefore substituted a tav for the heh . There is no need to place a dagesh in the tet . The word ve-karat (will befall) in and evil will befall you (Deut. 31:29) is similar. The word am (people) is here a feminine. Compare, ha-am (the people) in the people that were therein, how they dwelt in security (Jud. 18:7) and ha-am (the people) in Why is this people of Jerusalem slidden back (Jer. 8:5). Its meaning is, but the sin will be upon you. Moses out of respect alluded to Pharaoh by saying that the sin would be on his people. That I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders (I Kings 1:21), And our enemies mock us as they please (Ps. 80:7), and Thus they exchanged their glory (Ps. 106:20) are similar.
BUT HE SAID. Your words did not avail, as Pharaoh was steadfast in the hardness of his heart.
GO THEREFORE NOW, AND WORK. Pharaoh said this to the officers, as they too were obligated to work.

DID SEE. This verse is connected to the verses that follow it. They saw themselves in dire straits because Pharaoh had said to them, Ye shall not diminish aught from your bricks, your daily task . Then they met Moses and Aaron and complained to them. The word otam (they) means themselves, their very bodies. Otam (themselves) in But the shepherds fed themselves (Ezek. 34:8) and oto (himself) in and he buried himself in the valley (Deut. 34:6) are similar. Rabbi Moses ben Balaam says that oto (it) in he shall bring it (oto) unto the door of the tent of meeting (Num. 6:13) is also similar. However, in my opinion its meaning is that the priest shall command to bring him.

AND THEY MET. The words “who were” are missing. Our text should be read as if written: who were standing. And Pharaoh dreams (Gen. 41:1) is similar. Its meaning is, and Pharaoh was dreaming. Similarly, and behold he was standing by the river ( Ibid. ). There are many other such instances in Scripture.
AND THEY SAID UNTO THEM: THE LORD LOOK. At the violence done to us, the responsibility for which falls upon you.

[YE HAVE MADE OUR SAVOUR TO BE ABHORRED IN THE EYES OF PHARAOH.] Note that the five senses are perceived in one place located above the forehead. Hence one sense is substituted for another sense, as in And the light is sweet (Eccles. 11:7). However, Rabbi Merinus says that its meaning is, we are as disgusting and abhorrent in his eyes as a foul odor.

AND MOSES RETURNED. Now a question: Why did Moses complain and say, Why is it that thou hast sent me? and Neither hast thou delivered Thy people at all after God told him, And I know that the king of Egypt will not give you leave to go (Ex. 3:19) until he performed all the signs that God commanded him? The answer is, Moses thought that Pharaoh would lighten Israel’s yoke as soon as he spoke to him. However, Pharaoh placed a heavier workload upon them. [WHEREFORE HAST THOU DEALT ILL WITH THIS PEOPLE?] Contrary to Your words, I have surely seen the affliction of My people (Ex. 3:7); And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians ( Ibid. ). [WHY IS IT THAT THOU HAST SENT ME] To harm Israel. Behold, I have not found an answer to give the officers.
FOR SINCE. From the day that I spoke to Pharaoh he hardened his yoke over them, as it is written, And the same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people (v. 6).
[NEITHER HAST THOU DELIVERED.] My very thought was that Pharaoh would begin to lighten their burden and You would begin to deliver them.
[HE HAS DEALT ILL WITH THIS PEOPLE.] The word hera (he has dealt ill) is a transitive verb. It is similar to here’u (they did worse) in they did worse than their fathers (Jer. 7:26).
